hope.name: Hope the blue whale
hope.pack:
# Hope the blue whale — knowledge pack

Every section ends with its source. Only sourced statements may be used as facts in narration.
Statements marked UNSOURCED are context for the writer and must not be stated as fact.

## Stranding
Hope was a juvenile female blue whale. She stranded on a sandbar at the mouth of Wexford Harbour, Ireland,
on the morning of 25 March 1891.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/news/2018/march/a-cetacean-relation.html

## Sale to the museum
The 4.5-tonne skeleton was sold to the Natural History Museum for £250.
Source: https://nhm.ac.uk/discover/news/2018/september/secret-history-of-hope-the-blue-whale-finally-revealed.html

## Mammal Hall
The skeleton hung in the museum's Mammal Hall from 1934.
Source: https://nhm.ac.uk/discover/news/2017/july/museum-unveils-hope-the-blue-whale-skeleton.html

## Move to Hintze Hall
The skeleton was moved to Hintze Hall and unveiled there in July 2017. In Hintze Hall she replaced the cast of
Dippy the Diplodocus, which stood there from 1979 until January 2017.
Source: https://nhm.ac.uk/discover/news/2017/july/museum-unveils-hope-the-blue-whale-skeleton.html

## Her name
She was named Hope "as a symbol of humanity's power to shape a sustainable future".
Source: https://nhm.ac.uk/discover/news/2017/july/museum-unveils-hope-the-blue-whale-skeleton.html

## Size
The skeleton is 25.2 metres long.
Source: https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/GAG_J9wcz31GXw

## Pose (UNSOURCED)
The skeleton has 221 bones and is posed in a diving lunge. (Secondary source only; do not state as fact.)

## Appearance (for visuals, not narration)
Hung from the ceiling of Hintze Hall, a high Romanesque hall with terracotta arches and stained glass, the
skeleton is suspended mid-dive above visitors. As a living animal she would have had deep blue-grey mottled skin
and a pale ribbed throat.
hope.photo_note: The visitor photographed the skeleton from the first-floor balcony of Hintze Hall, looking across at it hanging mid-dive above a crowd.

sophie.name: Sophie the Stegosaurus
sophie.pack:
# Sophie the Stegosaurus — knowledge pack

Every section ends with its source. Only sourced statements may be used as facts in narration.
Statements marked UNSOURCED are context for the writer and must not be stated as fact.

## Who she is
Sophie is a Stegosaurus stenops, 150 million years old.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/press-office/press-releases/world_s-most-complete-stegosaurus-goes-on-show.html

She lived about 150 million years ago, in the Jurassic Period, in what is now Wyoming, USA. She is one of the most
complete Stegosaurus skeletons ever found; most Stegosaurus skeletons that are found are incomplete. She is on
display in the museum's Earth Hall.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/stegosaurus-brought-to-life.html

## Discovery
She was found in spring 2003 at Red Canyon Ranch, Wyoming, by Bob Simon, who runs a dinosaur quarry there.
He found her nearly fully connected skeleton buried at the top of a hill while expanding the quarry, and excavation took three weeks.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/press-office/press-releases/world_s-most-complete-stegosaurus-goes-on-show.html

## Completeness and size
She was found virtually complete; only the left arm and the base of the tail are missing. She is 560 cm long
and 290 cm tall, about the size of a 4x4, with over 300 bones. Her 19 back plates and four tail spikes are the
most complete set ever discovered.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/press-office/press-releases/world_s-most-complete-stegosaurus-goes-on-show.html

## Her skull
Her skull bones are three-dimensional and separate from one another, making it one of the most scientifically
valuable dinosaur skulls ever found, useful for studying how she ate and how hard she bit.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/press-office/press-releases/world_s-most-complete-stegosaurus-goes-on-show.html

## Coming to London
She arrived at the museum in December 2013. The museum's director thanked 70 generous donors, with particular
thanks to Jeremy Herrmann, for making the acquisition possible. She is named in honour of his daughter, Sophie
Herrmann. She went on display inside the Exhibition Road entrance from 4 December 2014, the first complete dinosaur
specimen to go on display at the museum in nearly 100 years. At the time of this 2014 press release she was the
only Stegosaurus in a public collection outside the USA; this may no longer be true, so do not
state it as a present-day fact. Her sex is not known; she was a young adult when she died.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/press-office/press-releases/world_s-most-complete-stegosaurus-goes-on-show.html

## How heavy she was
Scientists built a digital model of her whole skeleton and each of her 360 bones. After allowing for the fact
that she was a young adult whose limbs were still growing faster than her body, two methods agreed she weighed
about 1,600 kg in life, roughly a small rhino.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/news/2015/march/weight-of-the-worlds-most-complete-stegosaurus-revealed.html

## How she lived
She walked on all fours. Her front legs were short and back legs long, so she could not run and walked slowly at
only a few miles an hour. Her bite was about as strong as a cow's or sheep's, and she probably ate ferns, cycads
and other tough plants. Her small head had teeth about the size of a little fingernail.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/stegosaurus-brought-to-life.html

## Her plates
The plates on her back are very large but thin and fragile. Defence is now thought unlikely; they may have been
for display or for controlling body temperature; the plates seem to have been filled with lots of blood vessels. The space in her hips stored
food substances; it was not a second brain.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/stegosaurus-brought-to-life.html

## Bone count (conflicting)
The press release says over 300 bones; the 2015 news story says 360. Use "over 300" if a number is needed.

## Completeness percentage (UNSOURCED)
Press coverage gives figures of 80-90% complete. No NHM page read gives a percentage; do not state one.

## Appearance (for visuals, not narration)
A dark brown fossil skeleton mounted on a low plinth in the Earth Hall, a tall atrium at the Exhibition Road
entrance. She stands on four legs with short front limbs and long hind limbs, so her back arches high over the
hips; a small low head on a short neck; a double row of large, thin, diamond-shaped plates along her spine; four
long spikes near the tail tip. In life (reconstructions, not known for certain): a heavy, slow, rhino-sized
plant eater in a Jurassic landscape of ferns and cycads.

sequoia.name: The giant sequoia slice
sequoia.pack:
# The giant sequoia slice — knowledge pack

Every section ends with its source. Only sourced statements may be used as facts in narration.
Statements marked UNSOURCED are context for the writer and must not be stated as fact.

## Age and height
The tree was 1,300 years old and 101 metres tall when it was felled in California.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/giant-sequoia-slice.html

## Rings
Tree rings form under the bark as a tree grows taller and thicker, and counting them estimates its age.
Conservation work revealed the slice's many rings, which show how long the tree lived.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/giant-sequoia-slice.html

## At the museum
The slice has been at the museum since 1893 and was on public display for more than a century as part of the
botany collections. It now stands on the upper balcony of Hintze Hall, in the eaves.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/giant-sequoia-slice.html

## Conservation
Before treatment the top was under a layer of dust about an inch thick, over cloudy old varnish and wax.
It took three conservators 12 weeks to clean and conserve the slice. Once it was clean, they applied a new
conservation-grade resin that is stable and reversible, so it can be removed later if needed.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/giant-sequoia-slice.html

## Forests then and now
When the sequoia was felled, nearly 70% of the world's land area was covered in trees and forest. After 100
years this had dropped to below 40%, with an estimated 15 billion trees being cut down every year.
Source: https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/giant-sequoia-slice.html

## Felling year (UNSOURCED / conflicting)
The NHM page gives the felling as 1893 in its text but a photo caption says 1891. Do not state a felling year.

## Exact diameter (UNSOURCED)
The slice's diameter is not given on the NHM page. Do not state it.

## Appearance (for visuals, not narration)
A very large, round cross-section of trunk stood on edge on the top balcony of Hintze Hall, under the hall's
terracotta arches and painted ceiling panels. The cut face is warm reddish-brown wood with hundreds of fine
concentric rings, newly cleaned and glossy; the edge is a thick, fibrous, cinnamon-red bark. A timeline of
history runs beside it. As a living tree: a colossal straight red-barked trunk rising out of a Californian
forest.

--- Segment 1 (15.0s) ---
[0.0-5.0s] extreme close-up / static. One slow brush stroke.. The slice's top edge under thick matte grey dust; a gloved hand pulls a soft brush once through it, exposing dark wood.
[5.0-10.0s] close-up / slow drift right. A swab glides across.. Cut face under a cloudy yellowish film; a cotton swab glides across, leaving a clearer reddish-brown strip.

  VO @1.0s: "Under this shine, there was once about an inch of dust."
  VO @5.5s: "Beneath it, cloudy old varnish and wax."
  VO @10.3s: "It took three conservators twelve weeks to clean me."
  SOUND: Quiet studio room tone.; Soft brush through dust; Swab whisper; music: Sparse low solo cello, slow sustained notes, warm and quiet; holds a low note across the cut, no fade.
--- Segment 2 (15.0s) ---
[15.0-20.0s] extreme close-up / slow push-in from the bark edge toward the centre. Light glides.. Cinnamon-red bark giving way to tightly packed glossy rings, warm light sliding along them.
[20.0-25.0s] medium shot / static. Light settles.. The whole clean slice upright, every ring crisp, warm even light, soft dark background, no setting visible.

  VO @25.3s: "Look up. Thirteen hundred years of rings, uncovered."
